name: Freedom Riders National Monument
author: author-E-2026-10-18
summary:
Freedom Riders National Monument has two units in and near Anniston, Alabama: the former Greyhound bus depot at 1031 Gurnee Avenue downtown, with the adjacent Mural Building, and the Bus Burning Site almost six miles west of central Anniston, 5.86 acres around the spot on the Old Birmingham Highway where a Greyhound bus was set on fire in front of Forsyth & Son Grocery. President Barack Obama proclaimed the monument on January 12, 2017; its stated purpose is to foster reconciliation and racial healing. [1] [2]

In the spring of 1961, small interracial bands of Freedom Riders set out to test whether bus stations in the Deep South were obeying Supreme Court decisions — Morgan v. Virginia (1946) and Boynton v. Virginia (1960) — against segregation in interstate travel. On Mother’s Day, May 14, a mob that included Ku Klux Klan members met the Greyhound in Anniston, broke its windows and slashed its tires. Some six miles out of town the tires gave out, and someone threw a firebomb inside. The attackers held the door shut; the riders escaped after a detective on board drew his revolver, and at Anniston Memorial Hospital many of the injured were refused treatment. Photographs of the burning bus appeared in hundreds of newspapers the next morning. [1] [2]

More than 400 Freedom Riders followed. On May 29, 1961, Attorney General Robert Kennedy petitioned the Interstate Commerce Commission, which ordered bus carriers and terminals serving interstate travel integrated by November 1, 1961. [1] [2]

black.html:
The seven Freedom Riders on the Greyhound were four Black and three White volunteers sponsored by the Congress of Racial Equality. They included CORE field secretary Joe Perkins, Jimmy McDonald, a Black folk singer from New York, and Hank Thomas, recruited by his Howard University roommate. [1]

After White men fired shotguns into the homes of two Black families and into St. John’s Methodist Church on Mother’s Day 1963, the city created a Human Relations Council; by that September “White” and “Colored” signs had come down from fountains and restroom doors, but two Black ministers who tried to integrate the public library were met by a mob of Klansmen; Rev. Reynolds was beaten. Willie Brewster was shot on his way home from the Anniston Pipe Foundry and died; the conviction of Hubert Damon Strange was, the 2023 landscape report says, “the first time during the civil rights era that a White person was convicted of killing a Black person in Alabama.” [1]

sources.title: Knott, Cultural Landscape Report: Freedom Riders NM (2023), ch. 2 Site History, pp. 2-16–2-17, 2-26–2-27

women.html: Genevieve Hughes, a White CORE field secretary, rode the Greyhound from Washington; Mae Frances Moultrie, a student at historically Black Morris College, joined the riders in Sumter, South Carolina. As riders lay choking from smoke on May 14, 12-year-old Janie Forsyth, a daughter of grocer Richard Forsyth, brought cups and buckets of water and tended to the injured, while attackers’ families in their Sunday clothes stood and watched. Decades later, as Janie Forsyth McKinney, she joined Freedom Riders Hank Thomas, Charles Person and Bill Harbour at the public meeting on the proposed monument, which drew more than 450 people. [1]
